questions.text: A company owns a manufacturing plant that is currently idle. The plant has a book value of $2,000,000 and could generate $350,000 annually if returned to production (net of all operating costs). Alternatively, the plant could be sold for $2,800,000. A third option is to lease it for $200,000 per year. If the company chooses to return the plant to production, what is the annual opportunity cost of that decision?

answers.text: $0 — book value is a sunk cost and opportunity cost equals the foregone benefit of the next best alternative
$2,000,000 — the book value of the plant is the opportunity cost of using it for production
$200,000 — the annual lease income foregone by choosing production over leasing is the opportunity cost
$800,000 — the difference between sale proceeds and book value is the opportunity cost

explanations.a: The statement that opportunity cost equals foregone benefit of the next best alternative is correct, but claiming it equals $0 is wrong. The next best alternative (leasing) generates $200,000 per year — this is the foregone benefit and equals the annual opportunity cost. Book value being a sunk cost is correct, but that doesn't mean opportunity cost is zero.
explanations.b: Book value is a sunk cost — the historical cost of the plant that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered regardless of the decision made. Sunk costs are irrelevant to forward-looking opportunity cost analysis. Using book value as opportunity cost is a common analytical error.
explanations.c: Opportunity cost = Value of the next best alternative foregone. The company has three options: (1) Production: $350,000 net annual benefit; (2) Lease: $200,000 annual rent; (3) Sell: $2,800,000 one-time proceeds (but this is a one-time event, not annual). Comparing the two ongoing annual alternatives, if the company chooses production over leasing, the opportunity cost is the $200,000 annual lease income foregone. The correct framing uses the next best alternative among the realistic alternatives in the same time frame. Note: selling at $2,800,000 would also need to be compared, but since the company has elected to keep the plant (implicit in the question), the annual opportunity cost of production is the foregone lease income of $200,000. The production option ($350,000) exceeds leasing ($200,000) so production is the economically superior ongoing use — but the opportunity cost of choosing production over leasing is still $200,000.
explanations.d: The $800,000 gain on sale ($2,800,000 − $2,000,000) is relevant to the sale decision but represents an annual opportunity cost only if the sale proceeds could generate an annual return. As stated, $800,000 is not the opportunity cost of the production decision — the opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative (leasing at $200,000 per year).

questions.text: A consumer goods company is evaluating an acquisition of a regional competitor with $80 million in revenue, $12 million in EBITDA, and $45 million in net assets. The acquisition price is $72 million. The industry trades at 6x EBITDA. Management claims $4 million of annual cost synergies achievable within 2 years. Evaluate whether the acquisition price is justified using the EBITDA multiple and synergy analysis.

answers.text: The acquisition is underpriced — net assets of $45 million prove the company is worth at least $45 million, and paying $72 million is only a 60% premium over book value
The acquisition is overpriced — paying $72 million for $12 million of EBITDA equals 6.0x, which matches the industry average; no premium should be paid for a regional competitor
The acquisition is clearly justified — any acquisition at or below industry EBITDA multiples automatically creates shareholder value

At $72 million, the acquirer is paying 6.0x standalone EBITDA — matching the industry multiple; synergies of $4 million increase pro-forma EBITDA to $16 million, implying an effective acquisition multiple of 4.5x on synergy-adjusted EBITDA; this supports the transaction if synergies are achievable, but the acquirer should stress-test synergy execution risk and the 2-year realization timeline before committing

explanations.a: Book value (net assets) is a poor proxy for fair value in most acquisition contexts. The value of a business comes from its future earnings power, not its balance sheet. Paying $72 million for $12 million of EBITDA and $45 million of net assets is not 'underpriced' simply because it exceeds book value — many acquisitions appropriately pay significant premiums to book.
explanations.b: Paying the industry average multiple (6.0x) is not inherently wrong — it may reflect the fair price for the standalone business without synergies. The analysis should also consider synergies, strategic fit, and growth prospects. Additionally, industry multiple analysis is one valuation method; the question is whether the combination creates value beyond the standalone price.
explanations.c: Paying at or below the industry multiple guarantees neither value creation nor destruction. Synergy assumptions, integration costs, financing costs (interest on acquisition debt), execution risk, and growth prospects all determine whether the acquisition ultimately creates shareholder value. An 'automatically creates value' conclusion is never appropriate for complex M&A transactions.
explanations.d: Multi-framework acquisition analysis: Standalone valuation: Acquisition price / EBITDA = $72M / $12M = 6.0x. Industry multiple = 6.0x. The acquirer is paying exactly the industry multiple — this is a reasonable starting point with no discount and no premium for control or synergies, which could mean: the seller negotiated effectively, or the acquirer has identified synergy value not yet reflected in the multiple. Synergy-adjusted valuation: Pro-forma EBITDA = $12M + $4M synergies = $16M. Effective multiple = $72M / $16M = 4.5x. At 4.5x on synergy-adjusted EBITDA vs. a 6.0x industry multiple, the acquisition creates significant value if synergies are realized. Risk assessment: synergy execution risk — the $4M estimate should be supported by specific cost identification (headcount overlap, facility consolidation, procurement savings); 2-year timeline — integration costs typically frontload, while synergies materialize later; sensitivity analysis: if only 50% of synergies materialize, effective multiple = $72M / $14M = 5.1x (still below industry). Conclusion: acquisition is potentially value-creating but contingent on synergy realization.
